source: Iron availability limits primary productivity in high-nutrient, low-chlorophyll (HNLC) regions which cover ~25% of the modern ocean habitat as demonstrated by numerous large-scale Fe fertilization experiments and natural Fe upwelling events invariably resulting in diatom-dominated phytoplankton blooms (Ardyna et al., 2019; de Baar, 2005; Martin et al., 1994).

claim: Phytotransferrin serves as the basis of a high-affinity ferric (Fe3+) iron binding and acquisition pathway.
source: Diatoms have convergently evolved phytotransferrin (pTF), which serves as the basis of a high-affinity ferric, Fe3+, iron binding, and acquisition pathway (McQuaid et al., 2018; Morrissey et al., 2015).

claim: Phytotransferrin sequences have a broad taxonomic distribution.
source: Phytotransferrin sequences have a broad taxonomic distribution and are abundant in marine transcriptomic datasets (Bertrand et al., 2015; Marchetti et al., 2012).

claim: Phytotransferrin sequences are abundant in marine transcriptomic datasets.
source: Phytotransferrin sequences have a broad taxonomic distribution and are abundant in marine transcriptomic datasets (Bertrand et al., 2015; Marchetti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to transcriptomic studies.

claim: Phytotransferrins are estimated to have emerged concurrently with the Neoproterozoic Oxygenation Event.
source: Phytotransferrins are estimated to have emerged concurrently with the NOE exemplifying the link between large environmental changes and molecular innovation (McQuaid et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to evolutionary analysis.

claim: The emergence of phytotransferrins exemplifies the link between large environmental changes and molecular innovation.
source: Phytotransferrins are estimated to have emerged concurrently with the NOE exemplifying the link between large environmental changes and molecular innovation (McQuaid et al., 2018).
evidence: This is an inference based on the timing of phytotransferrin evolution.

claim: Phytotransferrins are phylogenetically related to FEA domain-containing proteins found in freshwater and marine single-celled algae.
source: They are phylogenetically related to Fe-assimilation (FEA) domain-containing proteins found in freshwater and marine single-celled algae, and represent functional analogues of iron delivery proteins transferrins (Behnke and LaRoche, 2020; Cheng et al., 2004; McQuaid et al., 2018; Scheiber et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to phylogenetic studies.

claim: Phytotransferrins represent functional analogues of iron delivery proteins transferrins.
source: They are phylogenetically related to Fe-assimilation (FEA) domain-containing proteins found in freshwater and marine single-celled algae, and represent functional analogues of iron delivery proteins transferrins (Behnke and LaRoche, 2020; Cheng et al., 2004; McQuaid et al., 2018; Scheiber et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: pTF from Phaeodactylum tricornutum was first identified as an iron deficiency-sensitive gene named ISIP2a.
source: pTF (Ensembl ID: Phatr3_J54465, UniProt ID: B7FYL2) from the model marine diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum (Bowler et al., 2008) was first identified as an iron deficiency-sensitive gene and named ISIP2a (iron starvation induced protein 2a) (Allen et al., 2008)
evidence: This is supported by citation to the original identification study.

claim: pTF expression is relatively high in iron-replete conditions.
source: pTF (Ensembl ID: Phatr3_J54465, UniProt ID: B7FYL2) from the model marine diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum (Bowler et al., 2008) was first identified as an iron deficiency-sensitive gene and named ISIP2a (iron starvation induced protein 2a) (Allen et al., 2008), although its expression is relatively high in iron-replete conditions as well (Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to transcriptomic data.

claim: pTF localizes to the cell surface and intracellular puncta, presumably endosomal vesicles.
source: pTF localizes to the cell surface and intracellular puncta, presumably endosomal vesicles (McQuaid et al., 2018), which is further supported by the presence of an endocytosis motif in the C-terminus of the protein (Lommer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to localization studies.

claim: pTF contains an endocytosis motif in the C-terminus.
source: pTF localizes to the cell surface and intracellular puncta, presumably endosomal vesicles (McQuaid et al., 2018), which is further supported by the presence of an endocytosis motif in the C-terminus of the protein (Lommer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to sequence analysis.

claim: In diatom pTF, dissolved labile ferric iron is coordinated synergistically with carbonate anion.
source: In diatom pTF, dissolved labile ferric iron is coordinated synergistically with carbonate anion (CO32-), a common feature of all transferrins (Cheng et al., 2004; McQuaid et al., 2018; Zak et al., 2002).
evidence: This is supported by citations to structural and biochemical studies.

claim: Synergistic coordination of iron with carbonate is a common feature of all transferrins.
source: In diatom pTF, dissolved labile ferric iron is coordinated synergistically with carbonate anion (CO32-), a common feature of all transferrins (Cheng et al., 2004; McQuaid et al., 2018; Zak et al., 2002).
evidence: This is established knowledge about transferrin biochemistry.

claim: Decline in seawater carbonate concentrations due to ocean acidification may negatively impact the phytotransferrin iron uptake system in diatoms.
source: Thus, decline in seawater carbonate concentrations due to ocean acidification caused by elevated atmospheric CO2 may negatively impact this prevalent iron uptake system in diatoms and other marine phytoplankton (McQuaid et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the carbonate requirement for pTF function.

claim: Fe3+ is highly insoluble.
source: Fe3+ is highly insoluble and conversion between Fe3+ and Fe2+ can lead to toxic reactive oxygen species causing damage to proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids (Cheng et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge in biochemistry.

claim: Conversion between Fe3+ and Fe2+ can lead to toxic reactive oxygen species.
source: Fe3+ is highly insoluble and conversion between Fe3+ and Fe2+ can lead to toxic reactive oxygen species causing damage to proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids (Cheng et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about iron chemistry and toxicity.

claim: Reactive oxygen species from iron redox cycling cause damage to proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids.
source: Fe3+ is highly insoluble and conversion between Fe3+ and Fe2+ can lead to toxic reactive oxygen species causing damage to proteins, lipids, and nucleic acids (Cheng et al., 2004).

claim: Precise control of iron internalization and intracellular trafficking is crucial for maintenance of cellular homeostasis.
source: Precise control of iron internalization and intracellular trafficking in either of its redox states is thus crucial for maintenance of cellular homeostasis (Philpott and Jadhav, 2019; Wang and Pantopoulos, 2011).

source: Human ferric iron-laden transferrin (Tf) bound to transferrin receptor is internalized via clathrin-mediated endocytosis.

claim: Endosome acidification leads to carbonate protonation and Tf conformational change resulting in iron release.
source: Endosome acidification leads to carbonate protonation and Tf conformational change resulting in iron release.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the transferrin cycle.

source: Fe3+ is then reduced by six-transmembrane epithelial antigen of prostate 3 (STEAP3), exported to the cytoplasm through divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1; also NRAMP2) or Zrt- and Irt-like protein (ZIP) 14, and offloaded to iron chaperones for distribution to cellular iron sinks (Bogdan et al., 2016; Eckenroth et al., 2011; Ohgami et al., 2005; Philpott and Jadhav, 2019; Wang and Pantopoulos, 2011).
evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian iron metabolism supported by citations.

claim: Fe2+ is exported to the cytoplasm through DMT1 or ZIP14.
source: Fe3+ is then reduced by six-transmembrane epithelial antigen of prostate 3 (STEAP3), exported to the cytoplasm through divalent metal transporter 1 (DMT1; also NRAMP2) or Zrt- and Irt-like protein (ZIP) 14, and offloaded to iron chaperones for distribution to cellular iron sinks (Bogdan et al., 2016; Eckenroth et al., 2011; Ohgami et al., 2005; Philpott and Jadhav, 2019; Wang and Pantopoulos, 2011).

claim: Iron is offloaded to iron chaperones for distribution to cellular iron sinks.

evidence: This is established knowledge about mammalian iron metabolism supported by citations.

evidence: This represents a knowledge gap that the study addresses.

claim: APEX2 is an engineered soybean ascorbate peroxidase.
source: To investigate the proximal proteomic neighborhood of P. tricornutum pTF, we employed APEX2, an engineered soybean ascorbate peroxidase that functions as a dual probe for electron microscopy and proximity proteomics (Hung et al., 2016; Lam et al., 2015; Martell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to the original APEX2 development papers.

claim: APEX2 functions as a dual probe for electron microscopy and proximity proteomics.
source: To investigate the proximal proteomic neighborhood of P. tricornutum pTF, we employed APEX2, an engineered soybean ascorbate peroxidase that functions as a dual probe for electron microscopy and proximity proteomics (Hung et al., 2016; Lam et al., 2015; Martell et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to APEX2 methodology papers.

claim: APEX2 is approximately 27 kDa in size.
source: When fused with a protein of interest (bait protein), the ~27 kDa APEX2 enzyme permits spatially resolved proteomic mapping by oxidizing biotin-phenol to short lived (<1 ms) phenoxyl radicals which can covalently react with electron-rich amino acid residues—primarily tyrosine—on the surface of nearby endogenous proteins.
evidence: This is a known property of APEX2.

claim: APEX2 oxidizes biotin-phenol to short-lived (<1 ms) phenoxyl radicals.
source: When fused with a protein of interest (bait protein), the ~27 kDa APEX2 enzyme permits spatially resolved proteomic mapping by oxidizing biotin-phenol to short lived (<1 ms) phenoxyl radicals which can covalently react with electron-rich amino acid residues—primarily tyrosine—on the surface of nearby endogenous proteins.
evidence: This is the established mechanism of APEX2 labeling.

claim: APEX2-generated phenoxyl radicals covalently react with electron-rich amino acid residues, primarily tyrosine.
source: When fused with a protein of interest (bait protein), the ~27 kDa APEX2 enzyme permits spatially resolved proteomic mapping by oxidizing biotin-phenol to short lived (<1 ms) phenoxyl radicals which can covalently react with electron-rich amino acid residues—primarily tyrosine—on the surface of nearby endogenous proteins.
evidence: This is the established mechanism of APEX2 labeling.

claim: The biotinylation radius in APEX2 experiments is estimated to be in the 10-20 nm range.
source: While the 'biotinylation radius' in APEX2 experiments is estimated to be in the 10–20 nm range, it should rather be seen as a 'probability gradient' where the likelihood of tagging decreases with distance away from the APEX2-tagged protein of interest (Gingras et al., 2019; Hung et al., 2016; Lam et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to APEX2 methodology papers.

claim: The biotinylation radius should be seen as a probability gradient where the likelihood of tagging decreases with distance.
source: While the 'biotinylation radius' in APEX2 experiments is estimated to be in the 10–20 nm range, it should rather be seen as a 'probability gradient' where the likelihood of tagging decreases with distance away from the APEX2-tagged protein of interest (Gingras et al., 2019; Hung et al., 2016; Lam et al., 2015).
evidence: This is an interpretation of APEX2 labeling characteristics supported by citations.

claim: APEX2 proteomic hits can include proteins that interact indirectly with the bait protein.
source: Proteomic hits can therefore include vicinal proteins which interact with the APEX2-tagged bait protein indirectly in addition to direct interactors of varying strength (Lundberg and Borner, 2019).
evidence: This is a characteristic of proximity labeling supported by citation.

claim: APEX2 can capture weakly and transiently interacting proteins.
source: Tha ability to capture weakly and transiently interacting proteins in a biological process of interest is a major advantage APEX2 offers over traditional pull-down approaches (Gingras et al., 2019).
evidence: This is a known advantage of APEX2 supported by citation.

claim: Swapping biotin-phenol for diaminobenzidine enables determination of fusion protein localization via electron microscopy.
source: Swaping biotin-phenol for diaminobendizine (DAB)—another APEX2 substrate—enables one to determine fusion protein localization via high-resolution electron microscopy making APEX2 a powerful bifunctional probe (Martell et al., 2017; Martell et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a known application of APEX2 supported by citations.

claim: APEX2 has been applied to investigate cellular compartments and processes in diverse model systems including mammalian cell culture, yeast, protists, and plant protoplasts.
source: APEX2 and related enzyme-based chemical biology tools have over the past decade been applied to investigate cellular compartments and processes in diverse model systems including mammalian cell culture, yeast, protists, and plant protoplasts (Gingras et al., 2019; Trinkle-Mulcahy, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citations to review articles on APEX2 applications.

claim: APEX2 was used to map proteomes associated with post-Golgi vesicle trafficking and endocytosis.
source: APEX2 was recently used to map proteomes associated with post-Golgi vesicle trafficking and endocytosis (Del Olmo et al., 2019; Otsuka et al., 2019) as well as receptor-mediated signaling (Paek et al., 2017), successes that are all directly pertinent to the goals of our study.
evidence: This is supported by citations to specific APEX2 studies.

claim: APEX2 was used to study receptor-mediated signaling.
source: APEX2 was recently used to map proteomes associated with post-Golgi vesicle trafficking and endocytosis (Del Olmo et al., 2019; Otsuka et al., 2019) as well as receptor-mediated signaling (Paek et al., 2017), successes that are all directly pertinent to the goals of our study.
evidence: This is supported by citation to a specific APEX2 study.

claim: Nearly 40 likely proximal proteins were identified through proximity-dependent proteomic mapping conducted in quintuplicate.
source: Here, we provide further evidence for P. tricornutum phytotransferrin pTF endocytosis, demonstrate correct subcellular localization and activity of its APEX2 fusion, and identify nearly 40 likely proximal proteins through a proximity-dependent proteomic mapping experiment conducted in quintuplicate.
evidence: This is a result from the mass spectrometry data presented in the study.

claim: This study represents the first application of APEX2 in a marine microbial model system.
source: To the best of our knowledge, this study represents the first application of APEX2 in a marine microbial model system (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the study based on the authors' knowledge of the literature.

claim: Three proteins from the chromosome 20 gene cluster are believed to act in association with endocytosed pTF downstream of ferric iron binding at the cell surface.
source: We then provide initial characterization, using dual fluorophore protein tagging fluorescence microscopy, phylogenetic, domain, and biochemical analyses, for three proteins expressed from a chromosomal gene cluster (pTF.CREG1, pTF.CatCh1, pTF.ap1) believed to act in association with endocytosed pTF downstream of ferric iron binding at the cell surface.
evidence: This is an inference based on the colocalization and proximity proteomics data.

claim: Bacterially expressed recombinant pTF.CREG1 was found to be catalytically dead.
source: Bacterially expressed recombinant pTF.CREG1 was found to be catalytically dead indicating it may have a regulatory, rather than enzymatic, role in pTF endocytosis, similar to functions proposed for human CREG1.
evidence: This is supported by the flavin reduction assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: pTF.CREG1 may have a regulatory, rather than enzymatic, role in pTF endocytosis.
source: Bacterially expressed recombinant pTF.CREG1 was found to be catalytically dead indicating it may have a regulatory, rather than enzymatic, role in pTF endocytosis, similar to functions proposed for human CREG1.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the lack of enzymatic activity and comparison to human CREG1.

claim: pTF.CatCh1 localization pattern suggests it might be a chloroplast-associated iron-binding protein.
source: Meanwhile, bioinformatic interrogation of pTF.CatCh1 and its localization pattern suggest it might be a chloroplast-associated iron-binding protein.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on localization data and sequence features.

claim: pTF-mCherry colocalizes with the membrane dye MDY-64 on the cell surface and within intracellular vesicles.
source: After labeling the fluorescent transconjugant cell line with 100 μM of the membrane dye MDY-64 for 10 min at room temperature, colocalized mCherry and MDY-64 signals were observed on the cell surface and within intracellular vesicles (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is supported by the fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: pTF-APEX2 fusion protein expression was confirmed in four transconjugant P. tricornutum cell lines.
source: Western blot with pTF-specific antibodies (McQuaid et al., 2018) confirmed the ~84.7 kDa fusion protein expression in four out of five tested transconjugant cell lines.
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The pTF-APEX2 fusion protein was present in the insoluble cell lysate fraction.
source: The protein was present in the insoluble cell lysate fraction further indicative of its membrane localization (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is supported by the western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: pTF-APEX2 expressing cells showed up to 40-fold higher resorufin signal than WT cells in the Amplex UltraRed assay performed on ice.
source: A resorufin (reaction product of Amplex UltraRed and APEX2) signal up to 4- and 40-fold above WT background was observed in experiments performed at room temperature (data not shown) and on ice (Figure 2D; Figure 2—source data 1), respectively, indicating active APEX2 with incorporated heme.
evidence: This is supported by the Amplex UltraRed assay data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: APEX2 was active only in the presence of both Amplex UltraRed and hydrogen peroxide.
source: APEX2 was active only in the presence of both Amplex UltraRed and hydrogen peroxide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) implying that endogenous H2O2 levels are not sufficient to drive APEX2-catalyzed reactions
evidence: This is supported by the control experiments shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Endogenous H2O2 levels in P. tricornutum are not sufficient to drive APEX2-catalyzed reactions.
source: APEX2 was active only in the presence of both Amplex UltraRed and hydrogen peroxide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) implying that endogenous H2O2 levels are not sufficient to drive APEX2-catalyzed reactions
evidence: This is an inference from the observation that exogenous H2O2 is required for APEX2 activity.

claim: The overall cell surface and intracellular milieu in P. tricornutum is permissive to the APEX2 catalytic cycle.
source: APEX2 was active only in the presence of both Amplex UltraRed and hydrogen peroxide (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C) implying that endogenous H2O2 levels are not sufficient to drive APEX2-catalyzed reactions, and that the overall cell surface and intracellular milieu in P. tricornutum is permissive to the APEX2 catalytic cycle.
evidence: This is an inference from the successful APEX2 activity in P. tricornutum.

claim: pTF-APEX2 is localized to the cell membrane and intracellular vesicles.
source: Tightly localized signal was observed on the cell membrane and in intracellular vesicles indicating that pTF-APEX2 fusion trafficked to the correct subcellular sites (Figure 3B).
evidence: This is supported by the electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Mitochondrial signal was observed in both WT and pTF-APEX2 cell lines subjected to the DAB reaction.
source: Additionally, we observed mitochondrial signal in WT and pTF-APEX2 cell lines subjected to the DAB reaction (Figure 3B; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is supported by the electron microscopy data shown in Figure 3B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: P. tricornutum proteome contains eight peroxidases with conserved catalytic amino acid residues found in ascorbate peroxidases.
source: Analysis of the P. tricornutum proteome revealed eight peroxidases with Arg38, His42, His163, and Asp208; catalytic amino acid residues that are conserved across all identified ascorbate peroxidases (APX) including soybean APX (Raven, 2003) and its derivative APEX2 (Figure 3—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Three P. tricornutum peroxidases contain proline at position 134 relative to APEX2.
source: Three of them contain proline in place of alanine at position 134 relative to APEX2, a substrate-binding loop mutation rendering APEX2 highly active (Lam et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment and citation to the APEX2 development paper.

claim: One P. tricornutum peroxidase is predicted to localize to mitochondria.
source: and another one is predicted to localize to mitochondria (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D–E).
evidence: This is supported by the localization prediction shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D-E.

claim: One or more endogenous APEX2-like peroxidases are responsible for the observed mitochondrial signal.
source: It is plausible that one or more of these endogenous APEX2-like peroxidases are responsible for the observed mitochondrial signal.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the presence of APEX2-like peroxidases and mitochondrial signal.

claim: Thirty-eight statistically significant proteins with APEX2/WT ratios of at least 1.5 were identified in the proximity proteomics experiment.
source: Thirty-eight statistically significant proteins (p value ≤ 0.05) with APEX2/WT ratios of at least 1.5 were identified (Figure 4B; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4B and Figure 4—source data 1.

claim: Endogenous biotinylated proteins were detected and had APEX2/WT ratios close to one.
source: Endogenous biotinylated proteins were also detected and had APEX2/WT ratios close to one, thus acting as an intrinsic pull-down control (Supplementary file 1—Table S1; Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data.

claim: Fourteen proteins with an APEX2/WT ratio of at least two were detected.
source: Fourteen proteins with an APEX2/WT ratio of at least two were detected.
evidence: This is supported by the mass spectrometry data.

claim: Nine of the 14 proteins with APEX2/WT ratio of at least two are known to be transcriptionally sensitive to iron availability.
source: Of these 14 proteins, nine are known to be transcriptionally sensitive to iron availability; this is also the case for an additional five proteins with APEX2/WT ratio of at least 1.5 (Figure 5—figure supplement 1—source data 1; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by comparison to transcriptomic data.

claim: pTF was present but not enriched in pTF-APEX2 proteomics samples.
source: We note that pTF was present, but not enriched, in our pTF-APEX2 proteomics samples (Figure 4—source data 1).
evidence: This is an observation from the mass spectrometry data.

claim: pTF may not have surface exposed amino acid residues permissive to biotinylation by APEX2-generated phenoxyl radicals.
source: One possible explanation for this result is that pTF may not have surface exposed amino acid residues that are permissive to biotinylation by APEX2-generated phenoxyl radicals and so its presence in all of our pull-down samples could be due to unspecific binding to streptavidin beads.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the lack of pTF enrichment.

claim: Five MS hits are predicted to be targeted to the chloroplast with low confidence by ASAFind.
source: Considering iron is critically involved in all of the major photosynthetic complexes—photosystem II, photosystem I, and cytochrome b6f (Rochaix, 2011)—we asked if some of the proteins are perhaps predicted to be targeted to the chloroplast. Indeed, five are, albeit with low confidence, by ASAFind (Gruber et al., 2015), including two (Phatr3_J51183 and Phatr3_J54986) that are part of a gene cluster on chromosome 20 and two (Phatr3_J41423 and Phatr3_J55031) that are known to associate with the P. tricornutum chloroplast (Figure 4C; Allen et al., 2012; Kazamia et al., 2019; Kazamia et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic prediction and citations to experimental localization studies.

claim: Two proteins (Phatr3_J41423 and Phatr3_J55031) are known to associate with the P. tricornutum chloroplast.
source: Considering iron is critically involved in all of the major photosynthetic complexes—photosystem II, photosystem I, and cytochrome b6f (Rochaix, 2011)—we asked if some of the proteins are perhaps predicted to be targeted to the chloroplast. Indeed, five are, albeit with low confidence, by ASAFind (Gruber et al., 2015), including two (Phatr3_J51183 and Phatr3_J54986) that are part of a gene cluster on chromosome 20 and two (Phatr3_J41423 and Phatr3_J55031) that are known to associate with the P. tricornutum chloroplast (Figure 4C; Allen et al., 2012; Kazamia et al., 2019; Kazamia et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental localization studies.

claim: The chromosome 20 gene cluster is transcriptionally sensitive to iron and silicon.
source: We focused on three proteins with APEX2/WT ratio of at least two—Phatr3 IDs: J51183 (hereafter pTF.CREG1), J52498 (hereafter pTF.CatCh1), and J54986 (hereafter pTF.ap1)—that are expressed from a previously identified iron- and silicon-sensitive gene cluster on chromosome 20 (Figure 5A; Allen et al., 2008; Sapriel et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous transcriptomic studies.

claim: pTF is located on chromosome 7, not co-located with the chromosome 20 gene cluster.
source: We note that pTF is not co-located with these genes, but instead lies on chromosome 7 (genomic location 1,000,053–1,001,833, forward strand).
evidence: This is based on genomic location information.

claim: All three genes from the chromosome 20 cluster exhibit a transcriptional profile similar to pTF.
source: All three genes exhibit a transcriptional profile similar to pTF (Figure 5—figure supplement 1)
evidence: This is supported by the transcriptomic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: pTF.CREG1 and pTF.ap1 are predicted to go to the chloroplast with low confidence.
source: two proteins (pTF.CREG1 and pTF.ap1) are predicted to go to the chloroplast (with low confidence as determined by ASAFind)
evidence: This is supported by bioinformatic prediction.

claim: pTF.CatCh1 and pTF.ap1 contain a C-terminal transmembrane domain.
source: and two (pTF.CatCh1 and pTF.ap1) contain a C-terminal transmembrane domain (Figure 4C; Supplementary file 1—Table S2).
evidence: This is supported by transmembrane domain prediction.

claim: pTF.CREG1 and pTF.CatCh1 colocalized with pTF in the chloroplast vicinity and on the chloroplast margin, respectively.
source: pTF.CREG1 and pTF.CatCh1 colocalized with pTF in the chloroplast vicinity and on the chloroplast margin, respectively (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is supported by the fluorescence microscopy data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: pTF.CREG1 homologs were identified across the tree of life.
source: pTF.CREG1 homologs were identified across the tree of life (Figure 6; Figure 6—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 6.

claim: Twelve amino acid residues are at least 90% conserved across all pTF.CREG1 homologs.
source: Further investigation of the protein sequence alignment underlying the phylogenetic tree revealed 12 amino acid residues that are at least 90% conserved across all homologs (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: Diatom pTF.CREG1 homologs form a crown group with proteins from other complex plastid-containing algae.
source: Diatom homologs can be seen in a crown group with proteins from other complex plastid-containing algae such as cryptophytes, haptophytes, pelagophytes, chlorarachniophytes, and dinoflagellates (Figure 6; Archibald, 2009; Füssy and Oborník, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 6.

claim: pTF.CREG1 and its paralog Phatr3_J10972 have approximately 50% amino acid sequence similarity.
source: pTF.CREG1 and its iron-insensitive paralog Phatr3_J10972—which phylogenetically cluster together—have ~50% amino acid sequence similarity
evidence: This is based on sequence comparison.

claim: pTF.CREG1 and Phatr3_J10972 belong to the flavin mononucleotide (FMN)-binding split barrel fold protein superfamily.
source: and belong to the flavin mononucleotide (FMN)-binding split barrel fold protein superfamily (SSF50475) according to their Ensembl Protists profiles.
evidence: This is based on domain annotation from Ensembl.

claim: pTF.CREG1 has a predicted N-terminal signal peptide ending in SGA.
source: pTF.CREG1 has a predicted N-terminal signal peptide ending in SGA that may be recognized by an endoplasmic reticulum-localized signal peptidase (Benham, 2012; Tuteja, 2005)
evidence: This is supported by signal peptide prediction and citations.

claim: pTF.CREG1 is likely modified by both N- and O-glycosylation.
source: and is likely modified by both N- and O-glycosylation, in line with human CREG1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 2A; Sacher et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by glycosylation site prediction and comparison to human CREG1.

claim: pTF.CREG1 contains a loop occluding the FMN-binding pocket similar to human CREG1.
source: Structural comparison between a pTF.CREG1 homology model created using Phyre2 web portal (Kelley et al., 2015) and the human CREG1 monomer (PDB ID: 1XHN; Sacher et al., 2005) supports our hypothesis that pTF.CREG1 also contains a loop preventing FMN binding (Figure 6—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is supported by structural modeling shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2B.

claim: pTF.CREG1 lacks at least one arginine amino acid residue required for terminal FMN phosphate binding.
source: Two arginine amino acid residues involved in binding the terminal FMN phosphate in S. cerevisiae pyridoxine 5′-phosphate oxidase (UniProt ID: P38075, PDB ID: 1CI0) are mutated to aspartic acid and methionine amino acid residues in human CREG1 (Sacher et al., 2005), and one of these two key arginine residues is absent from pTF.CREG1 (Figure 6—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment and structural comparison shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3A.

claim: Recombinant pTF.CREG1 exhibited no flavin reductase activity.
source: The Co2+-bound protein fraction (Figure 6—figure supplement 4B) exhibited no flavin reductase activity as measured by the oxidation of NADPH in the presence of potential flavin substrates flavin mononucleotide (FMN) and riboflavin (Figure 6—figure supplement 2C; Figure 6—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the enzymatic assay data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2C.

claim: pTF.CREG1 does not bind FMN and does not reduce flavins in an NADPH-dependent manner.
source: In conclusion, our homology modeling analyses and enzymatic assays indicate that pTF.CREG1 does not bind FMN and does not reduce flavins in an NADPH-dependent manner, respectively, both in agreement with our current knowledge about human CREG1.
evidence: This is supported by the structural modeling and enzymatic assay data.

claim: pTF.CatCh1 homologs were identified only in diatoms and other single-celled heterokonts.
source: In contrast to pTF.CREG1, pTF.CatCh1 homologs were identified only in diatoms and other single-celled heterokonts (Figure 7A; Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 7A.

claim: pTF.CatCh1 is a ~37.4 kDa (349 AAs) large protein with a predicted signal peptide.
source: pTF.CatCh1 is a ~37.4 kDa (349 AAs) large protein with a predicted signal peptide (AAs 1–26) ending in ASA
evidence: This is based on protein sequence analysis.

claim: pTF.CatCh1 is paralogous to ISIP2b.
source: This protein is paralogous to the iron starvation induced protein 2b (ISIP2b/Phatr3_J54987) whose gene lies adjacently to pTF.CatCh1 in the same chromosome 20 gene cluster (Figure 5A).
evidence: This is based on phylogenetic analysis and genomic location.

claim: pTF.CatCh1 and ISIP2b share three CXC and one CXXC motifs.
source: They share three CXC and one CXXC motifs typical of metal-binding, redox-active, and iron–sulfur cluster-containing proteins (Figure 7B; Blaby-Haas et al., 2014; Fomenko and Gladyshev, 2003; Poole, 2015; Przybyla-Toscano et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by sequence alignment shown in Figure 7B and citations.

claim: One CXC motif and the CXXC motif are conserved across all but two pTF.CatCh1 homologs.
source: One of the CXC motifs and the CXXC motif are conserved across all but two homologs in our phylogenetic analysis (Figure 7B; Figure 7—figure supplement 1A)
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 7B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A.

claim: pTF.CatCh1 contains a total of 20 cysteine amino acid residues.
source: With additional 12 cysteines conserved between pTF.CatCh1 and ISIP2b, pTF.CatCh1 contains a total of 20 cysteine amino acid residues (all between AAs 34 and 226).
evidence: This is based on sequence analysis.

claim: Six of the 20 cysteines in pTF.CatCh1 are 100% conserved across all homologs.
source: Six of these 20 are 100% conserved across all homologs (Figure 7B).
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 7B.

claim: pTF.ap1 homologs are present in diatoms and other marine microeukaryotes.
source: Phylogenetic characterization was performed with pTF.ap1 as well and numerous homologs with at least five highly conserved motifs were identified in diatoms and other marine microeukaryotes, including chlorophytes, cryptophytes, and haptophytes (Figure 7—figure supplement 2A–B; Figure 7—figure supplement 2—source data 1).
evidence: This is supported by the phylogenetic tree shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2A.

claim: pTF.ap1 homologs contain five 100% conserved cysteine amino acid residues.
source: These pTF.ap1 homologs contain five 100% conserved cysteine amino acid residues, two of which are shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B
evidence: This is supported by the sequence alignment shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2B.

claim: pTF.ap1 homologs contain 100% conserved tyrosine, histidine, and aspartic acid residues.
source: as well as 100% conserved tyrosine, histidine, and aspartic acid residues, indicating this protein may also be redox-active and/or have a metal ion processing role (Dokmanić et al., 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the conserved residues and citation.

claim: MDY-64 labeling data provide the first direct evidence that diatom pTF is associated with intracellular membranous compartments.
source: McQuaid et al., 2018 observed pTF in intracellular puncta, showed that the clathrin-mediated endocytosis inhibitor Pitstop 2 reduces iron (Fe) uptake rates, visualized vesicles after adding iron to an iron-limited WT P. tricornutum culture stained with the membrane dye FM 1–43, but our MDY-64 labeling data provide the first direct evidence that diatom pTF is indeed associated with intracellular membranous compartments.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty of the MDY-64 labeling data compared to previous work.

claim: An order of magnitude higher signal-to-noise ratio was detected when live cells were reacted on ice as opposed to room temperature in the Amplex UltraRed assay.
source: In our Amplex UltraRed assay experiments, an order of magnitude higher signal-to-noise ratio (i.e. resurofin signal in pTF-APEX2 expressing versus WT P. tricornutum cells) was detected when live cells were reacted on ice as opposed to on room temperature
evidence: This is supported by the Amplex UltraRed assay data.

claim: Endogenous P. tricornutum peroxidases are largely inhibited on ice, but not exogenous APEX2.
source: suggesting endogenous P. tricornutum peroxidases, but not exogenous APEX2, are largely inhibited on ice.
evidence: This is an inference from the temperature-dependent signal-to-noise ratio.

claim: Performing APEX2 assays on ice may represent a generalizable experimental strategy for mesophilic microeukaryotic phytoplankton model systems.
source: This is notable as it indicates that performing APEX2 assays on ice may represent a generalizable experimental strategy for mesophilic microeukaryotic phytoplankton model systems.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the success in P. tricornutum.

claim: C-terminal tagging of pTF with APEX2 resulted in the expected cell surface and vesicular fusion protein localization away from mitochondria.
source: Nevertheless, C-terminal tagging of pTF with APEX2 resulted in the expected cell surface and what appeared to be vesicular fusion protein localization away from mitochondria indicating no spatial overlap between endogenous APEX2-like enzymes and pTF-APEX2.
evidence: This is supported by the electron microscopy data.

claim: Many MS hits with elevated APEX2/WT ratios have functional annotations for proteins expected to play a role in endosomal iron assimilation.
source: Many of the latter have functional annotations for proteins we might expect to play a role in endosomal iron assimilation, and many have previously been shown to have iron-sensitive transcripts, both of which further support this notion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the functional annotations and transcriptomic data.

claim: Iron metabolism genes in P. tricornutum, including pTF, are highly expressed at night.
source: Considering iron metabolism genes in P. tricornutum, including pTF, are highly expressed at night, proteomic maps with improved spatial and temporal resolution may emerge from proximity-dependent proteomic mapping experiments conducted with synchronized cell lines sampled at different timepoints throughout diel cycle (Huysman et al., 2014; Lundberg and Borner, 2019; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to transcriptomic data.

claim: TurboID has been successfully implemented in model plants Arabidopsis thaliana and Nicotiana benthamiana.
source: The successful implementation of TurboID—an engineered biotin ligase for proximity proteomics (Branon et al., 2018)—in model plants Arabidopsis thaliana (Kim et al., 2019; Mair et al., 2019) and Nicotiana benthamiana (Zhang et al., 2019) suggests its adoption in existing and emerging single-celled marine phytoplankton model systems, including diatoms, is likely (Faktorová et al., 2020; Falciatore et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to TurboID studies in plants.

claim: TurboID is an iron-independent protein.
source: TurboID is an iron-independent protein and could thus be particuarly valuable to further advance iron metabolism studies in P. tricornutum.
evidence: This is established knowledge about TurboID.

claim: The chromosome 20 gene cluster is transcriptionally upregulated in iron-deplete and silicic-acid-replete conditions.
source: Functionally uncharacterized gene cluster on chromosome 20 we zoomed in on is transcriptionally upregulated in iron-deplete (Allen et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2016) and silicic-acid-replete (Sapriel et al., 2009) conditions corroborating a known link between iron and silicon metabolism in diatoms (Brzezinski et al., 2015; Durkin et al., 2012; Hutchins and Bruland, 1998; Leynaert et al., 2004).
evidence: This is supported by citations to transcriptomic studies.

claim: There is a known link between iron and silicon metabolism in diatoms.
source: Functionally uncharacterized gene cluster on chromosome 20 we zoomed in on is transcriptionally upregulated in iron-deplete (Allen et al., 2008; Smith et al., 2016) and silicic-acid-replete (Sapriel et al., 2009) conditions corroborating a known link between iron and silicon metabolism in diatoms (Brzezinski et al., 2015; Durkin et al., 2012; Hutchins and Bruland, 1998; Leynaert et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Physically clustered functionally related genes are a hallmark of prokaryotic biology.
source: Physically clustered functionally related genes are a hallmark of prokaryotic biology and operon-like genomic elements have been described in fungi and plants (Nützmann et al., 2018; Osbourn and Field, 2009)
evidence: This is established knowledge in genomics supported by citations.

claim: Operon-like genomic elements have been described in fungi and plants.
source: Physically clustered functionally related genes are a hallmark of prokaryotic biology and operon-like genomic elements have been described in fungi and plants (Nützmann et al., 2018; Osbourn and Field, 2009)
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomics studies.

claim: Identifying and characterizing gene clusters in marine diatom genomes is in its relative infancy.
source: however, identifying and characterizing them in marine diatom genomes is in its relative infancy.
evidence: This is an assessment of the state of the field.

claim: Genes encoding light harvesting fucoxanthin-chlorophyll-binding proteins (FCPs) are co-located on chromosome 2 in P. tricornutum.
source: For example, genes encoding light harvesting fucoxanthin-chlorophyll-binding proteins (FCPs) are co-located on chromosome 2 in P. tricornutum (Bhaya and Grossman, 1993)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a genomic study.

claim: A compact ~7 kbp gene cluster encoding enzymes for domoic acid neurotoxin production was characterized in Pseudo-nitzschia multiseries.
source: and a compact ~7 kbp gene cluster encoding enzymes for domoic acid neurotoxin production was characterized in a cosmopolitan diatom Pseudo-nitzschia multiseries (Brunson et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a genomic study.

claim: Diatom genomes have likely been extensively shaped by horizontal gene transfer.
source: Given that diatom genomes have likely been extensively shaped by horizontal gene transfer (Bowler et al., 2008; Diner et al., 2017)
evidence: This is supported by citations to genomic studies.

claim: Some yeast species acquired iron acquisition-enabling operon-like genomic elements via horizontal operon transfer from an ancient bacterium.
source: it is interesting to note that some yeast species acquired iron acquisition-enabling operon-like genomic elements via horizontal operon transfer (HOT) from an ancient bacterium (Kominek et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a genomic study.

claim: In humans, endosome acidification causes structural rearrangements in transferrin and protonation of carbonate anion leading to ferric iron release.
source: In humans, endosome acidification causes structural rearrangements in the transferrin protein and protonation of synergistically coordinated carbonate anion leading to ferric iron release (Cheng et al., 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about the transferrin cycle supported by citation.

claim: Two putative proton pumps were present in the mass spectrometry data: Phatr3_J23497 and Phatr3_J27923.
source: Two putative proton, H+, pumps were present in our mass spectrometry data: Phatr3_J23497—predicted as a P-type ATPase—and Phatr3_J27923—a vacuolar-type H+-ATPase subunit A.
evidence: This is based on the mass spectrometry data and functional annotation.

claim: Multisubunit V-ATPases regulate pH homeostasis in virtually all eukaryotes.
source: Multisubunit V-ATPases regulate pH homeostasis in virtually all eukaryotes and are known to function as endosome acidifying protein complexes (Finbow and Harrison, 1997; Maxson and Grinstein, 2014)
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citations.

claim: Phatr3_J27923 is a candidate protein involved in acidification of phytotransferrin-rich endosomes in P. tricornutum.
source: which makes Phatr3_J27923 a candidate protein involved in acidification of phytotransferrin-rich endosomes in P. tricornutum.
evidence: This is an inference based on the known function of V-ATPases and the MS data.

claim: V-ATPase transcripts were overrepresented in diatoms following iron enrichment.
source: Notably, V-ATPase transcripts were overrepresented in diatoms following iron enrichment, possibly to account for an increase in the number of endosomes associated with pTF-driven iron acquisition (Marchetti et al., 2012)
evidence: This is supported by citation to a transcriptomic study.

claim: V-ATPase was shown to be involved in diatom silica deposition vesicle (SDV) acidification.
source: and V-ATPase was shown to be involved in diatom silica deposition vesicle (SDV) acidification (Hildebrand et al., 2018; Yee et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to experimental studies.

claim: Human CREG1 is a glycoprotein involved in embryonic development, growth, differentiation, and senescence.
source: Human cellular repressor of E1A-stimulated genes 1 (CREG1) is a glycoprotein involved in embryonic development, growth, differentiation, and senescence as part of the endosomal-lysosomal system (Ghobrial et al., 2018; Schähs et al., 2008).
evidence: This is established knowledge about human CREG1 supported by citations.

claim: Human CREG1 forms a homodimer unable to bind FMN in vitro.
source: Contrary to evolutionarily related flavin mononucleotide (FMN)-binding split barrel fold oxidases and oxidoreductases such as pyridoxine 5′-phosphate (PNP) oxidase, an enzyme involved in vitamin B6 metabolism (Musayev et al., 2003), CREG1 forms a homodimer unable to bind FMN in vitro suggesting it does not act as an enzyme in vivo (Sacher et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about human CREG1 supported by citation.

claim: The lack of FMN in human CREG1 is due to a short loop protruding into the FMN-binding pocket and specific amino acid substitutions.
source: The lack of FMN in human CREG1 is due to a short loop protruding into the FMN-binding pocket at the dimer interface, and aspartic acid and methionine amino acid residues replacing the corresponding two yeast PNP oxidase (PDB ID: 1CI0) arginines responsible for binding the terminal FMN phosphate (Sacher et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about human CREG1 structure supported by citation.

claim: pTF.CREG1 was proposed to be central to sustained growth of iron-limited P. tricornutum cells.
source: CREG1-like protein pTF.CREG1 was proposed to be central to sustained growth of iron-limited P. tricornutum cells (Allen et al., 2008) or to serve as a cell surface iron receptor (Lommer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: CREG transcripts were more common in diatom transcriptomes from the Southern Ocean than non-Southern Ocean regions.
source: CREG transcripts were more common in diatom transcriptomes from the Southern Ocean as opposed to non-Southern Ocean regions indicating these proteins are important in coping with iron limitation in this major high-nutrient, low-chlorophyll (HNLC) zone (Moreno et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a transcriptomic study.

claim: Secreted glycosylated human CREG1 delays G1/S cell cycle phase transition via direct interaction with M6P/IGF2R.
source: Secreted glycosylated human CREG1 was shown to delay G1/S cell cycle phase transition via direct interaction with mannose 6-phosphate/insulin-like growth factor II receptor (M6P/IGF2R), a receptor internalized via clathrin-mediated endocytosis (Di Bacco and Gill, 2003; Ghosh et al., 2003; Han et al., 2009).
evidence: This is established knowledge about human CREG1 function supported by citations.

claim: Human CREG1-mediated cellular growth inhibition partially depends on a tetrapeptide motif within the FMN binding pocket-occluding loop.
source: This cellular growth inhibition was demonstrated to, at least partially, depend on a tetrapeptide motif within an FMN binding pocket-occluding loop (Sacher et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a functional study.

claim: Internalization of the human transferrin-transferrin receptor complex is a regulated kinase-activity-dependent process.
source: Internalization of the human transferrin-transferrin receptor complex is not a constitutive, but rather a regulated kinase-activity-dependent process (Cao et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge about transferrin endocytosis supported by citation.

claim: pTF.CREG1 may serve as a checkpoint to regulate phytotransferrin endocytosis in response to iron availability.
source: We currently hypothesize that pTF.CREG1 may serve as a 'checkpoint' to keep phytotransferrin endocytosis at a low level in iron-replete conditions, but when iron is scarce instead positively regulate this pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the data and comparison to human CREG1.

claim: A second transcriptional peak for pTF.CREG1 occurs in iron-deplete medium approximately 8 hr prior to the pTF peak.
source: Indeed, transcriptomics experiments show that a second transcriptional peak for pTF.CREG1 occurs in iron-deplete medium approximately 8 hr prior to the pTF peak, a transcriptional dynamic which would be consistent with our hypothesis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1; Smith et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by the transcriptomic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Glycosylation in human CREG1 appears to be important for interaction with its cognate receptor.
source: Given that glycosylation in human CREG1 appears to be important for interaction with its cognate receptor (Han et al., 2011; Sacher et al., 2005; Schähs et al., 2008), posttranslational modifications, perhaps glycosylation(s), of pTF.CREG1 may further drive this regulatory activity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on human CREG1.

claim: The presence of Phatr3_J10972, an iron-insensitive pTF.CREG1 paralog, suggests CREG-like proteins are implicated in diverse endocytosis pathways in single-celled eukaryotic phytoplankton.
source: The presence of Phatr3_J10972, an iron-insensitive pTF.CREG1 paralog, in the P. tricornutum genome suggests that CREG-like proteins are implicated in diverse endocytosis pathways in single-celled eukaryotic phytoplankton.
evidence: This is an inference based on the existence of a paralog with different expression pattern.

claim: The association between iron-sensitive pTF.CREG1 and phytotransferrin implies a specific pTF.CREG1 function in non-reductive iron uptake.
source: However, the association between iron-sensitive pTF.CREG1 and phytotransferrin in P. tricornutum implies a specific pTF.CREG1 function in non-reductive iron uptake.
evidence: This is an inference based on the colocalization and proximity proteomics data.

claim: The outermost complex plastid membrane in diatoms corresponds to the chloroplast endoplasmic reticulum (cER) and is continuous with the nuclear envelope.
source: The outermost complex plastid membrane in diatoms corresponds to the chloroplast endoplasmic reticulum (cER) and is continuous with the nuclear envelope (Gibbs, 1981; Prihoda et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about diatom cell biology supported by citations.

claim: Nuclear-encoded P. tricornutum proteins destined for the periplastidial compartment are first cotranslationally imported into the cER lumen.
source: Nuclear-encoded P. tricornutum proteins destined for the periplastidial compartment (vastly reduced endosymbiont cytoplasm between the inner two and the outer two complex plastid membranes) are first cotranslationally imported into the cER lumen (Grosche et al., 2014; Peschke et al., 2013).
evidence: This is established knowledge about diatom protein targeting supported by citations.

claim: pTF.CatCh1 may get to its final destination via cotranslational membrane insertion.
source: Our microscopy results show that pTF.CatCh1 is localized on the chloroplast margin, perhaps anchored to the outer chloroplast (cER) membrane with its C-terminal transmembrane domain, thus raising a possibility that pTF.CatCh1 gets to its final destination via cotranslational membrane insertion.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the localization data and known protein targeting mechanisms.

claim: The CXXC motif in pTF.CatCh1 is preceded by an aspartic acid residue resulting in DCXXC which is known to be permissive to binding divalent metal ions.
source: This motif in pTF.CatCh1 is preceded by an aspartic acid residue resulting in DCXXC which is known to be particularly permissive to binding divalent metal ions (Figure 7—figure supplement 1A; Banci et al., 2002; Banci et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by sequence analysis and citations to structural studies.

claim: Disordered protein domains are mediators of protein-protein interactions and play an important role in the formation of protein complexes.
source: Given the nearly completely conserved C(X)XC motifs and additional six 100% conserved cysteine residues, it is conceivable they are critical to pTF.CatCh1 activity. Based on the fluorescence microscopy data, the conserved cysteine amino acid residues and cysteine-containing motifs, and given that disordered protein domains—two are predicted to flank the pTF.CatCh1 transmembrane domain—are mediators of protein-protein interactions and play an important role in the formation of protein complexes (Uversky, 2015b; Uversky, 2016)
evidence: This is established knowledge about disordered proteins supported by citations.

claim: pTF.CatCh1 may serve as a metallochaperone that binds ferrous iron downstream of endosomal ferric iron reduction.
source: First, pTF.CatCh1 may serve as a metallochaperone that binds ferrous, Fe2+, iron downstream of the endosomal ferric, Fe3+, iron reduction step, and directs it to the chloroplast interior.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the sequence features and localization data.

claim: Metallochaperones are intracellular proteins responsible for protecting and guiding metal ions to correct metalloenzyme sinks.
source: Metallochaperones are intracellular proteins responsible for protecting and guiding metal ions on their way to correct metalloenzyme sinks (O'Halloran and Culotta, 2000).
evidence: This is established knowledge about metallochaperones supported by citation.

claim: pTF.CatCh1 may recruit pTF to the chloroplast periphery via one of its C-terminal disordered regions.
source: Second, pTF.CatCh1 may recruit pTF to the chloroplast periphery via one of its two C-terminal disordered regions flanking the predicted transmembrane domain, and thus serve as a docking site for iron-laden pTF.
evidence: This is a speculative hypothesis based on the sequence features and localization data.

claim: pTF.CatCh1 could recruit pTF via the 'fly-casting mechanism' which involves binding-induced protein folding.
source: It could achieve this via the 'fly-casting mechanism' which involves binding-induced protein folding (Shoemaker et al., 2000).
evidence: This is a speculative mechanism supported by citation to a structural biology concept.

claim: The observed colocalization of pTF.CatCh1 with pTF may indicate that Fe3+ can be offloaded directly from pTF to pTF.CatCh1.
source: The observed colocalization of pTF.CatCh1 with pTF may indicate that Fe3+ can be offloaded directly from pTF to pTF.CatCh1 which would imply an additional, non-endosomal, intracellular Fe3+ reduction step.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the colocalization data.

claim: A chloroplast-associated Fe3+ reduction pathway mediated by Fe3+ chelate reductase FRO7 is present in Arabidopsis thaliana.
source: Notably, a chloroplast-associated Fe3+ reduction pathway mediated by Fe3+ chelate reductase FRO7 is present in Arabidopsis thaliana (Jeong et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study in Arabidopsis.

claim: pTF.CatCh1 exhibits a second transcriptional peak in iron-deplete medium approximately 16 hr prior to the pTF peak.
source: Similarly to pTF.CREG1, pTF.CatCh1 exhibits a second transcriptional peak in iron-deplete medium approx. 16 hr prior to the pTF peak (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by the transcriptomic data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Chloroplasts are the most iron-rich system in plant cells.
source: Chloroplasts are the most iron-rich system in plant cells (López-Millán et al., 2016).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Iron serves as an essential cofactor for the photosynthetic electron transfer chain, chlorophyll biosynthesis, and chloroplast protein import.
source: Iron—in particular in the form of iron–sulfur (Fe–S) clusters—serves as an essential cofactor for the photosynthetic electron transfer chain, chlorophyll biosynthesis, and chloroplast protein import (Balk and Schaedler, 2014; Marchand et al., 2018; Soll and Schleiff, 2004).
evidence: This is established knowledge about chloroplast iron metabolism supported by citations.

claim: A complex vesicle-based system possibly in perpetual dynamic exchange with cytosolic vesicles is present in chloroplasts.
source: A complex vesicle-based system possibly in perpetual dynamic exchange with cytosolic vesicles is present in chloroplasts (Hertle et al., 2020; Lindquist and Aronsson, 2018)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on chloroplast vesicle trafficking.

claim: An endoplasmic reticulum to Golgi to chloroplast protein trafficking pathway exists.
source: an endoplasmic reticulum to Golgi to chloroplast protein trafficking pathway exists (Radhamony and Theg, 2006; Villarejo et al., 2005)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on protein trafficking.

claim: 'Kiss and run' mechanism allows erythroid cell mitochondria to access iron via direct interaction with transferrin-rich endosomes.
source: 'Kiss and run' mechanism that allows erythroid cell mitochondria to access iron via direct interaction with transferrin-rich endosomes further underscores this idea (Hamdi et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a study on iron trafficking in mammalian cells.

claim: ISIP1 gene expression in P. tricornutum and other marine microeukaryotes is induced by iron limitation.
source: ISIP1 (iron starvation induced protein 1; Phatr3_J55031) gene expression in P. tricornutum and other marine microeukaryotes is induced by iron limitation (Allen et al., 2008; Kazamia et al., 2018; Marchetti et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to transcriptomic studies.

claim: P. tricornutum ISIP1 has a role in siderophore-bound iron uptake.
source: P. tricornutum ISIP1—the second most enriched protein in our MS dataset—has a role in siderophore-bound iron uptake and colocalizes with phytotransferrin (pTF) adjacently to the chloroplast in an 'iron-processing compartment' (Kazamia et al., 2019; Kazamia et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: ISIP1 colocalizes with phytotransferrin adjacently to the chloroplast in an 'iron-processing compartment'.
source: P. tricornutum ISIP1—the second most enriched protein in our MS dataset—has a role in siderophore-bound iron uptake and colocalizes with phytotransferrin (pTF) adjacently to the chloroplast in an 'iron-processing compartment' (Kazamia et al., 2019; Kazamia et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to localization studies.

claim: FBP1 is central to the carbonate-independent iron acquisition pathway in P. tricornutum.
source: FBP1 (Phatr3_J46929)—iron-sensitive siderophore ferrichrome-binding protein with punctate intracellular localization and central to the carbonate-independent iron acquisition pathway in P. tricornutum (Allen et al., 2008; Coale et al., 2019)—was another highly enriched protein in our dataset
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: The internalization pathways for inorganic and organic iron in P. tricornutum may be physically coupled intracellularly.
source: indicating the internalization pathways for inorganic (i.e. phytotransferrin-bound) and organic (i.e. siderophore-bound) iron in P. tricornutum may be physically coupled intracellularly and directed to iron-accumulating vesicles close to the chloroplast.
evidence: This is an inference based on the enrichment of both ISIP1 and FBP1 in the MS data.

claim: Metal homeostasis by discrete membranous compartments is widespread in nature.
source: Metal homeostasis by such discrete membranous compartments is widespread in nature (Blaby-Haas and Merchant, 2014).
evidence: This is established knowledge supported by citation.

claim: Copper- and zinc-storing compartments (cuprosomes and zincosomes) are present in Chlamydomonas reinhardtii.
source: Copper- and zinc-storing compartments—cuprosomes and zincosomes, respectively—are present in the model chlorophyte microalga Chlamydomonas reinhardtii (Aron et al., 2015; Hong-Hermesdorf et al., 2014; Merchant, 2019)
evidence: This is supported by citations to studies on metal homeostasis in Chlamydomonas.

claim: Lipid-bound iron-accumulating ferrosome compartments exist in diverse bacteria and archaea.
source: and lipid-bound iron-accumulating ferrosome compartments exist in diverse bacteria and archaea (Grant and Komeili, 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citation to a review on ferrosomes.

claim: FBAC5 was shown to be localized to the P. tricornutum pyrenoid.
source: Finally, the most enriched protein in our MS dataset was FBAC5 (Phatr3_J41423)—iron-sensitive iron-independent class I fructose-biophosphate aldolase—which was shown to be localized to the P. tricornutum pyrenoid—proteinaceous RuBisCO-containing subchloroplastic organelle—and proposed to link Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle activity with the CO2 concentrating mechanism (Allen et al., 2012; Matsuda et al., 2017).
evidence: This is supported by citations to localization studies.

claim: FBAC5 is one of the most reliable markers for diatom iron stress.
source: FBAC5 is one of the most reliable markers for diatom iron stress as demonstrated by laboratory culture (Cohen et al., 2018; Lommer et al., 2012), microcosm incubation (Cohen et al., 2017a; Cohen et al., 2017b), and field studies (Bertrand et al., 2015)
evidence: This is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Fructose-biphosphate aldolases (FBAs) are glycolytic enzymes known for their ability to moonlight.
source: Fructose-biphosphate aldolases (FBAs) are glycolytic enzymes known for their ability to moonlight (Boukouris et al., 2016), a term for proteins with multiple physiologically relevant functions encoded by one polypeptide chain (Jeffery, 2018).
evidence: This is established knowledge about FBAs supported by citations.

claim: Moonlighting FBAs have roles in actin cytoskeleton dynamic, cellular growth arrest, and apoptosis in human cancer cell lines.
source: Moonlighting FBAs have roles in actin cytoskeleton dynamic, cellular growth arrest, and apoptosis (in human cancer cell lines; Gizak et al., 2019), transcriptional regulation (in yeast; Cieśla et al., 2014), and endosome acidification via direct interaction with vacuolar-type ATPase (in a mouse cell line; Merkulova et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to functional studies.

claim: FBAC5 acting outside of the P. tricornutum chloroplast, perhaps in the endosomal-lysosomal system, is possible.
source: These reported non-catalytic FBA activities suggest that FBAC5 acting outside of the P. tricornutum chloroplast, perhaps in the endosomal-lysosomal system as our data would imply, is possible.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the moonlighting functions of FBAs and the MS data.

claim: It remains to be determined which protein is responsible for intracellular ferric iron reduction in P. tricornutum.
source: Importantly, it remains to be determined which protein is responsible for intracellular ferric, Fe3+, iron reduction in P. tricornutum, activity that would be consistent with the non-reductive cell surface ferric, Fe3+, iron uptake proposed for phytotransferrin (pTF) (McQuaid et al., 2018; Morrissey et al., 2015).
evidence: This represents a knowledge gap identified by the study.

claim: Neither of the five proteins with clear ferric reductase annotation nor additional five hypothetical ferric reductases were present in the mass spectrometry data.
source: Perhaps notably, neither of the five proteins with clear ferric reductase annotation (FRE1–5, Phatr3 IDs: J54486, J46928, J54940, J54409, J54982) nor additional five hypothetical ferric reductases (Coale et al., 2019; Smith et al., 2016) were present in our mass spectrometry data.
evidence: This is an observation from the MS data.

claim: Enzymatic Fe3+ reduction may happen later in the pathway and/or in a separate subcellular compartment.
source: Further proximity-dependent proteomic mapping experiments will be essential for determining the full set of proteins in the non-reductive iron acquisition pathway in P. tricornutum as enzymatic Fe3+ reduction may happen later in the pathway and/or in a separate subcellular compartment.
evidence: This is a speculative inference about why ferric reductases were not detected.
